title: “DO NOT WORRY ABOUT TOMORROW” — JESUS NEVER TOLD YOU TO STOP PLANNING
paragraphs: “DO NOT WORRY ABOUT TOMORROW” — JESUS NEVER TOLD YOU TO STOP PLANNING
You can prepare for tomorrow without carrying tomorrow. The difference may be exactly what your exhausted soul needs to hear tonight.
There is a version of tomorrow already living inside your head.
It has conversations that have not happened.
Bills that are not yet due.
Test results you have not received.
Doors that have not closed.
People who have not left.
Problems that have not arrived.
Failures that have not occurred.
And somehow…
you are already exhausted from surviving them.
Your body is sitting in today, but your mind has traveled three weeks ahead.
You are lying in bed, but internally you are running.
Calculating.
Rehearsing.
Predicting.
“What if I lose the job?”
“What if the money does not come?”
“What if my child makes the wrong decision?”
“What if the doctor calls?”
“What if this relationship falls apart?”
“What if I never recover?”
“What if God does not come through the way I desperately need Him to?”
And perhaps the strangest part is that you call it “being responsible.”
You tell yourself you are planning.
You tell yourself you are preparing.
You tell yourself that thinking about the problem one hundred more times might finally produce control.
But somewhere between preparation and obsession, planning became panic.
And somewhere between wisdom and fear, tomorrow became your master.
Then Jesus says something that almost sounds impossible:
“Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself.”
That is Matthew 6:34 in the King James Version.

But if you have ever read those words while staring at overdue bills, raising children, running a business, trying to save money, preparing for an uncertain future, or simply attempting to behave like a responsible adult, you may have quietly wondered:
Jesus… are You really telling me not to think about tomorrow?
No.
And understanding what He actually said may set someone free tonight.
Matthew was written in Greek, and the crucial words in Matthew 6:34 read:
“μὴ οὖν μεριμνήσητε εἰς τὴν αὔριον”
Mē oun merimnēsēte eis tēn aurion.
The heart of the sentence is the verb μεριμνάω — merimnaō.
It carries the sense of being anxious, worried, troubled, or consumed with care.
That matters.
Jesus was not condemning foresight.
He was confronting anxiety.
He was not saying, “Never make plans.”
He was saying, in effect, “Do not surrender your heart to anxious preoccupation about tomorrow.”
There is an enormous difference.
Planning looks toward tomorrow and asks, “What can I wisely do today?”
Worry looks toward tomorrow and asks, “How can I control everything that might happen?”
Planning can finish its work and sleep.
Worry keeps holding meetings at 2:13 in the morning.
Planning makes a budget.
Worry checks the bank account fourteen times.
Planning prepares for the medical appointment.
Worry mentally attends your own funeral before the doctor has even given you a diagnosis.
Planning teaches your children wisdom.
Worry tries to control every decision they will make for the next twenty years.
Planning says, “If the Lord wills, this is what I intend to do.”
Worry whispers, “Unless I personally hold every piece together, everything will collapse.”
And maybe that is why worry is so exhausting.
You were never designed to be God.
Read the entire movement of Jesus’ words in Matthew 6:25–34 and something beautiful happens.
Jesus points upward.
Look at the birds.
Then outward.
Look at the flowers.
Then inward.
Look at your anxiety.
Then upward again.
Look at your Father.
The birds are not Jesus’ argument against work. Birds spend enormous energy gathering food.
The flowers are not His argument against reality. Grass withers.
His argument is about the character of the Father.
“Your heavenly Father knoweth that ye have need of all these things.”
Before Jesus tells frightened people not to worry, He gives them something stronger than positive thinking.
He gives them a Father.
That changes everything.
Christian peace is not pretending tomorrow will be painless.
Jesus never promised that.
In fact, the final words of Matthew 6:34 destroy the shallow idea that Christianity means nothing difficult will happen:
“ἀρκετὸν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἡ κακία αὐτῆς.”
Arketon tē hēmera hē kakia autēs.
“Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.”
Jesus acknowledges trouble.
That is what makes His command so astonishing.
He does not say, “Do not worry because nothing bad will happen.”
He essentially says, “Today already contains enough trouble. Do not drag tomorrow’s trouble into it as well.”
Somebody needs to read that twice.
You may be suffering today from something that has not happened.
You may be grieving an imaginary funeral.
Fighting an imaginary argument.
Enduring an imaginary bankruptcy.
Surviving an imaginary rejection.
Feeling the pain of an imaginary betrayal.
You have borrowed trouble from a day God has not yet given you.
And because you borrowed tomorrow’s trouble, you are spending today’s strength on something that may never happen.
But there is another side to this.
Some Christians have misunderstood Jesus’ words and treated irresponsibility as faith.
“I do not need to save. God will provide.”
“I do not need to prepare. God will handle it.”
“I do not need to make wise decisions. I am trusting Jesus.”
That is not what Matthew 6 teaches.
The Bible repeatedly commends wisdom, diligence, stewardship, preparation, and thoughtful action.
Joseph prepared Egypt for seven years of famine.
Proverbs points us toward the ant that prepares its provisions.
Jesus Himself spoke about counting the cost before building a tower.
James did not condemn making plans; he corrected the arrogance of planning as though God were irrelevant: “If the Lord will, we shall live, and do this, or that.”
Biblical faith is not careless.
It simply refuses to make an idol out of control.
So make the appointment.
Build the emergency fund.
Study for the examination.
Prepare the presentation.
Write the business plan.
Buy what is needed.
Save wisely.
Teach your children.
Think about retirement.
Set the alarm.
Apply for the job.
Have the difficult conversation.
Plan for tomorrow.
Just do not worship tomorrow.
Do not give tomorrow authority over your peace today.
Do not let a calendar date that has not arrived become more powerful in your imagination than the Father who is already there.
Because perhaps this is the deeper wound beneath our worry:
We do not merely fear tomorrow.
Sometimes we fear that when tomorrow comes, God will somehow not be enough.
That is where this becomes painfully personal.
You can believe God exists and still struggle to trust Him.
You can sing worship songs on Sunday and panic on Monday.
You can quote Scripture publicly and secretly imagine catastrophe at night.
You can tell everybody else, “God has a plan,” while privately wondering whether His plan for you has somehow fallen apart.
Faith and fear can fight inside the same chest.
Peter knew Jesus and still sank.
The father in Mark 9 cried, “Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
So if you are anxious tonight, Jesus is not standing over you with folded arms, disgusted that you are struggling.
Look at how He speaks in Matthew 6.
“Your heavenly Father…”
He brings the anxious heart back to relationship.
Your Father knows.
Your Father sees.
Your Father has not misplaced you.
And this does not mean you will receive everything you want.
It does not mean every illness disappears.
It does not mean every business succeeds.
It does not mean every relationship survives.
It does not mean every prayer receives the answer you imagined.
Christian hope is much deeper than “Everything will work out exactly how I want.”
Christian hope says:
Whatever tomorrow contains, Christ will still be Christ.
And ultimately, your greatest problem was never tomorrow.
It was sin.
The deepest disaster threatening humanity was not unemployment, sickness, rejection, debt, aging, loneliness, or death.
It was separation from a holy God because of sin.
And that is exactly where the Gospel becomes more than motivational advice.
Jesus did not come merely to make anxious people calmer.
He came to save sinners.
The Christ speaking about tomorrow in Matthew 6 was walking toward a cross.
There would come a tomorrow when He would be betrayed.
A tomorrow when He would be falsely accused.
A tomorrow when Roman soldiers would beat Him.
A tomorrow when nails would tear through flesh.
A tomorrow when darkness would fall.
A tomorrow when the sinless Son of God would give His life for sinners.
And Jesus knew it was coming.
Yet He continued obeying the Father.
That is not denial.
That is trust.
At Calvary, the One who taught us not to be mastered by tomorrow carried something infinitely heavier than tomorrow.
He carried our sin.
Our shame.
Our rebellion.
Our guilt.
Our record.
Our scandal.
The secret things.
The things nobody knows.
The things you wish you could erase.
The decisions you would give almost anything to undo.
And this is why Gospel Warrior keeps returning to the same truth:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin acceptable.
Not by teaching us to excuse rebellion.
He rewrites the story through repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and grace purchased by His blood.
At the cross, sin is not minimized.
It is judged.
And grace is not cheap.
It cost Christ everything.
Then came another tomorrow.
The stone was rolled away.
The tomb was empty.
Jesus Christ rose.
And suddenly the future of everyone who belongs to Him could never again be defined merely by what happens tomorrow.
Because resurrection had entered the story.
Maybe that is the tomorrow you have forgotten.
You have imagined a hundred terrible tomorrows.
Have you remembered the final one?
The day when faith becomes sight.
The day when Christ gathers His people.
The day when death does not get the final sentence.
The day when every redeemed sinner discovers that Jesus was more faithful than fear ever allowed them to imagine.
Until then, He gives us today.
Daily bread.
Notice the language.
Not monthly bread.
Not lifetime bread.
“Give us this day our daily bread.”
There is something almost offensive about daily dependence to people obsessed with control.
We want lifetime guarantees.
God often gives daily grace.
We want the entire map.
He gives enough light for the next faithful step.
We want to know how everything ends.
Jesus says, “Follow Me.”
Maybe you do not need an answer for the next ten years tonight.
Maybe you need grace for Monday.
Maybe you do not need enough strength to survive everything your imagination can manufacture.
Maybe you need strength for this conversation.
This appointment.
This decision.
This temptation.
This lonely evening.
This single act of obedience.
Today.
Because tomorrow has not asked you to live it yet.
So stop demanding tomorrow’s grace before tomorrow arrives.
When tomorrow becomes today, the God who met you today will still be God.
That does not make planning unnecessary.
It makes panic unnecessary.
Prepare what you can.
Entrust what you cannot.
Then breathe.
Not because life is predictable.
Because Jesus is faithful.
And perhaps you have been carrying something while reading this.
Something specific.
A name appeared in your mind.
A diagnosis.
A deadline.
A debt.
A marriage.
A child.
A mistake.
A decision.
A secret fear you have not admitted to anyone.
Do not hide behind religious language.
Bring it to Christ.
If you need to repent, repent.
If you need to forgive, forgive.
If you need to apologize, apologize.
If you need to make a responsible plan, make one.
If you need professional help, seek it.
If there is work God has placed in front of you, do it.
But after obedience has done everything obedience can do…
release the outcome.
Your clenched fist cannot control tomorrow anyway.
Open it.
“Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you.”
There is the invitation.
Not pretending.
Casting.
Not suppressing.
Surrendering.
Not “I am fine.”
“Father, I am afraid.”
There is a difference between surrender and denial.
And maybe somebody reading this has been pretending for too long.
Not because typing a sentence magically removes anxiety.
It does not.
But sometimes confession is the moment we stop pretending.
No explanation required.
And if Christ has already carried you through a tomorrow you once thought would destroy you, tell somebody.
There is someone scrolling through these words who may desperately need evidence that another believer cried, trembled, prayed, survived—and discovered that God had not abandoned them.
Do not keep that testimony locked inside you.
And think of one person who is living three months ahead in fear right now.
You know who they are.
The friend whose marriage is shaking.
The mother worried about her child.
The father carrying financial pressure silently.
The believer whose faith is tired.
The person waiting for medical results.
The person smiling online while privately falling apart.
Better yet, send this directly to them.
Not merely to help an algorithm.
One share can place Scripture in front of someone you may never have known was desperate for it.
Because anxiety has a strange habit of forgetting yesterday’s lessons when tomorrow becomes frightening again.
Come back when your mind starts running ahead of grace.
Read Matthew 6 again.
Look at the birds again.
Look at the flowers again.
Look at the Father again.
Then look at Christ.
And I want to say this carefully because biblical truth matters more than fundraising:
You do not buy a blessing.
And no faithful Christian ministry should pressure you into giving.

Scripture teaches that Christian giving should be willing rather than compelled: “Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7.
But voluntary financial support is a real way believers can help Gospel-centered work continue and expand.
Call it what Scripture clearly allows us to call it:
Generosity.
Partnership.
Support.
Giving from a willing heart.
A practical decision to help Gospel-centered ministry continue.
And if you decide before God that this is where you want part of your Christian giving to go, then give freely, prayerfully, joyfully, and without compulsion.
But the deepest reason to stay connected should never be merchandise.
It should be Jesus.
Stay close to Scripture.
Stay teachable.
Stay hungry for Christ.
Your support can help keep Gospel-centered content moving outward.
Your share can put truth on another screen.
Your tag can reach the person who would never have searched for this themselves.
Your comment can become a testimony somebody else needed to read.
But Jesus alone saves.
Jesus alone deserves the glory.
And that distinction must never be blurred.
So tomorrow morning, plan.
Make your list.
Set your goals.
Check your calendar.
Go to work.
Pay what you can.
Save what you can.
Prepare wisely.
Make the phone call.
Schedule the appointment.
Do the next responsible thing.
But before you walk into tomorrow, remember:
You are not walking there alone.
The Father you trust today will not disappear at midnight.
Christ will already be Lord when morning arrives.
Grace will already be there.
And whatever tomorrow eventually brings, it will never be stronger than the Savior who conquered the grave.
So tonight…
put tomorrow back where it belongs.
Not in your hands.
In His.
You do not have to carry tomorrow tonight—the hands already holding tomorrow still bear the scars that prove how far His love was willing to go for you.
